clusters.state_of_play: Meta launched an AI image generation tool called Muse on Tuesday that allows Instagram users to tag public profiles and generate AI images using faces from those accounts' posts. Public Instagram users are not notified when their posts are used. Following widespread backlash over privacy and consent — including criticism from a Hollywood union — Meta has discontinued the Muse Image feature, saying it 'misses the mark' on users' privacy. Separately, the European Commission on Friday issued a preliminary charge sheet finding Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act over 'addictive' design features on Instagram and Facebook — specifically video autoplay and infinite scroll — which regulators say cause compulsive use and harm users' physical and mental health. Meta faces a fine of up to 6% of global turnover. Additionally, Meta is appealing a landmark Los Angeles jury verdict that found it liable for social media addiction among young users.

Health workers are threatening to walk off the job over delayed payments, while misinformation is fuelling violent attacks on treatment facilities, health workers, and burial operations. clusters.state_of_play: The former Pfizer HQ at 235 E. 42nd St., a 37-story tower undergoing office-to-apartment conversion into over 1,600 units, was found at risk of collapse after structural columns buckled and floors sagged beneath a 10-story horizontal expansion of the building. This triggered evacuation of the building and 148 guests at the neighboring Hampton Inn Grand Central, along with traffic restrictions and closures affecting a busy Midtown stretch near Grand Central for over a day. FDNY drone images confirm the interior damage. The tower has since been stabilized enough for repairs and some residents have been allowed to return. Developer Nathan Berman (MetroLoft) has publicly downplayed the incident, calling it a freak accident limited to a 20-by-20-foot localized section. City records show safety complaints about the building dating to spring 2025, including complaints about falling debris, many of which were dismissed by emergency teams that responded to them. The incident has now drawn a criminal investigation by the NYC Department of Investigation and the Manhattan district attorney's office, though the inquiry is in an early stage and its focus remains unclear. The incident has raised broader questions about NYC's office-to-apartment conversion trend.

ledger.what_new: Barcelona recorded its highest temperature in 112 years; French nuclear reactor shut down due to extreme heat.

clusters.state_of_play: Western Europe recorded its hottest June ever, with temperatures 3.06°C (or ~5.5°C by another Copernicus metric) above average, driven by carbon pollution and an exceptionally strong 'Super El Niño'. The UK is in its third heatwave of the year, with UK A&E attendances hitting a record 81,264 in June and school absences in England reaching nearly 20% during the heatwave — June 26 was the highest daily absence rate of the 2025/26 academic year. Wildfires are ravaging France and Spain; a French nuclear reactor has shut down due to extreme heat. Barcelona recorded its highest temperature in 112 years, with some Spanish stations hitting 44°C. Estimates suggest the continent-wide death toll from June's heatwave could exceed 20,000, with ~5,000 excess deaths in Germany alone and thousands more in France, Spain and Belgium. Ireland has issued high temperature warnings. Globally, June 2025 was the second-hottest June on record (16.54°C), behind June 2024 (16.66°C). ECMWF expert Tim Stockdale warns the 2025 El Niño may break records for strength. Ground-level ozone concentrations were continuously elevated across Europe during the June heatwave, posing potentially deadly health risks; the London mayor issued a rare high air pollution alert following extreme heat warnings from 22 June, and ozone pollution is expected to rise again as the UK enters its third heatwave.

clusters.title: This Summer, Midtown Manhattan Is Taking Center Stage

items.title: This Summer, Midtown Manhattan Is Taking Center Stage

clusters.state_of_play: The former Pfizer HQ at 235 E. 42nd St., a 37-story tower undergoing office-to-apartment conversion into over 1,600 units, was found at risk of collapse after structural columns buckled and floors sagged beneath a 10-story horizontal expansion of the building. This triggered evacuation of the building and 148 guests at the neighboring Hampton Inn Grand Central, along with traffic restrictions and closures affecting a busy Midtown stretch near Grand Central for over a day. FDNY drone images confirm the interior damage. The tower has since been stabilized enough for repairs and some residents have been allowed to return. Developer Nathan Berman (MetroLoft) has publicly downplayed the incident, calling it a freak accident limited to a 20-by-20-foot localized section. City records show safety complaints about the building dating to spring 2025, including complaints about falling debris, many of which were dismissed by emergency teams that responded to them. The incident has now drawn a criminal investigation by the NYC Department of Investigation and the Manhattan district attorney's office, though the inquiry is in an early stage and its focus remains unclear. The incident has raised broader questions about NYC's office-to-apartment conversion trend.

clusters.title: Unstable NYC building case may make converting offices into apartments harder

items.title: Unstable NYC building case may make converting offices into apartments harder

clusters.state_of_play: The former Pfizer HQ at 235 E. 42nd St., a 37-story tower undergoing office-to-apartment conversion into over 1,600 units, was found at risk of collapse after structural columns buckled and floors sagged beneath a 10-story horizontal expansion of the building. This triggered evacuation of the building and 148 guests at the neighboring Hampton Inn Grand Central, along with traffic restrictions and closures affecting a busy Midtown stretch near Grand Central for over a day. FDNY drone images confirm the interior damage. The tower has since been stabilized enough for repairs and some residents have been allowed to return. Developer Nathan Berman (MetroLoft) has publicly downplayed the incident, calling it a freak accident limited to a 20-by-20-foot localized section. City records show safety complaints about the building dating to spring 2025, including complaints about falling debris, many of which were dismissed by emergency teams that responded to them. The incident has now drawn a criminal investigation by the NYC Department of Investigation and the Manhattan district attorney's office, though the inquiry is in an early stage and its focus remains unclear. The incident has raised broader questions about NYC's office-to-apartment conversion trend.
